# About the Dataset {#sec-about-the-dataset .unnumbered}

This textbook is built around one integrated dataset, the Charles River Accounting Dataset. Rather than using multiple databases at different levels of complexity, this book uses a single company that students learn deeply over the course of the book. Every chapter builds on the same data environment, so a customer order analyzed in an Excel chapter appears in the general ledger queried in a SQL chapter and surfaces in a Power BI dashboard built later. This continuity reinforces learning and mirrors real professional practice, where accountants work within one company's data for extended periods.


## The Company

Charles River is a fictional mid-size company situated in the greater Boston area that designs and sells home furnishings through wholesale and direct-to-business channels. The product catalog includes furniture, lighting, textiles, and decorative accessories organized into product families that students can visualize and compare analytically. Charles River manufactures selected product lines in-house from raw materials and packaging, purchases other finished goods from outside suppliers, and warehouses inventory across multiple locations. The company also operates an interior design services practice that bills customers by the hour, giving students a second revenue model within the same business. Charles River maintains a full chart of accounts with cost center tracking across its departments.

This hybrid operating model is a deliberate design choice. A company that both buys and makes products, sells both goods and services, and manages both manufacturing labor and salaried professionals creates the range of accounting transactions that students need to encounter. Students can compare purchased products with manufactured products, trace how customer demand drives purchasing and production decisions, analyze how labor supports both operations and services, and see how all of these activities flow into the general ledger.


## The Business Cycles

Charles River's operations are organized into business cycles that students will recognize from their accounting courses. The Order-to-Cash cycle traces customer demand from sales orders through shipments, invoicing, and cash receipts. The Design Services cycle, a branch of the revenue cycle, covers hourly consulting engagements that are staffed, approved, and billed monthly, creating a second revenue path alongside product sales. The Procure-to-Pay cycle covers replenishment from requisition through purchasing, goods receipt, and vendor payment. The Manufacturing cycle turns selected products into finished goods through planning, work orders, material issue, labor support, and production completion. The Payroll cycle processes employee time records into payroll registers, payments, and remittances. The Manual Journals and Close cycle handles accruals, reclassifications, and period-end adjustments through manual journal entries. Every one of these cycles ultimately flows into the general ledger, where the entire company's financial activity is recorded.


## From Business Events to the General Ledger

The dataset is designed so that students can follow a transaction from the business event that created it to its posting in the general ledger. Every ledger entry records the source document that produced it, which lets students see exactly how a sales invoice becomes revenue and a shipment becomes cost of goods sold, how a goods receipt becomes an inventory entry, or how a payroll run becomes wage expense. This source-to-ledger traceability is one of the most valuable features of the dataset for teaching purposes, and the chapters return to it repeatedly, from assessing data quality to testing journal entries in audit analytics.


## Progressive Introduction

The book does not ask students to work with the entire database from the beginning. Part I introduces the company, its business model, and the way its data is organized, and its tutorials already work in the Excel workbook: exploring the tables, testing data quality, and tracing a sale from the order to the ledger. The Excel chapters in Part II begin with a focused set of sales and general ledger tables and later draw on the planning and purchasing tables for budgeting and audit tests. The SQL chapters in Part III expand into purchasing and manufacturing data, where relational joins become essential. The Power BI chapters in Part IV build data models that span the business cycles, and the capstone cases in Part V require students to move fluently across the full dataset and all three tools, choosing the tool that each step of a problem calls for.


## Distribution Formats

The dataset is provided in three formats. The SQLite database supports the SQL chapters and the population-level work in the capstone cases of Part V, and it works with DB Browser for SQLite, the free database tool the SQL chapters use. The Excel workbook supports the tutorials in Part I, the spreadsheet work in the Excel chapters, and the Power BI chapters, which load its Tables directly. The CSV package suits any other tool, and it is a faster way to load the largest tables into Power BI. All three formats contain identical data, so students work with the same underlying information regardless of which tool a given chapter uses. Direct links to all three formats are available on the [Downloads](#sec-downloads) page.

For documentation of the tables, fields, and relationships, visit the [Charles River Accounting Dataset website](https://charlesriver.accountinganalyticshub.com/). All dataset changes and updates will be posted on that website. Each edition of this book is verified against one release of the dataset, and the [Downloads](#sec-downloads) page names it and links to its files, so that your results match the chapters.
